narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 52.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is a borderline estimate—slightly above a coin flip—not a definite prediction, but it was enough to place your application on the denied side.

The most important factor was your LSAT score, which worked in your favor. At 42, it is above the average of 37.18 among admitted students, so this was the strongest signal pushing the model toward a pass prediction. The second most important factor, however, worked against you: your Year 3 decile of 2 is well below the admitted-student average of 5.79, indicating comparatively low academic standing in your third year and pushing the prediction toward bar failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential factor and also counted against you: at 2.40, it is below the admitted-student average of 3.23, though its influence was smaller than your third-year rank.

Your middle family income, full-time status, and Year 1 decile were not among the top three drivers, so the denial centers mainly on the tension between a strong LSAT and weaker academic indicators, especially your third-year standing and undergraduate GPA.

Next, ask admissions whether you can discuss the academic record, especially any context for your third-year rank and GPA. Consider taking additional coursework or otherwise demonstrating readiness for rigorous law study, and seek advising on whether to reapply after strengthening that record or apply to programs where your LSAT strength is weighted more heavily.
